summary:
AgroNASA is an interactive agricultural decision-support web platform designed to help farmers and agronomists build climate resilience through data-driven crop rotation planning. Focusing initially on the semi-arid agricultural zones of San Luis, Argentina, the platform transforms 26 years of historical satellite and meteorological records from NASA POWER (2000–2025) into actionable field strategies.

By selecting a geographic zone on an interactive map and entering plot conditions and previous campaign history, users receive tailored crop rotation strategies—balancing soil conservation, risk diversification, and productivity. Powered by a Python/FastAPI agronomic scoring engine and a React/Leaflet frontend, AgroNASA evaluates local drought probabilities, heatwaves, frost hazards, and optimal planting windows against crop-specific phenological requirements.

Unlike black-box tools, AgroNASA provides complete transparency: farmers can compare strategies side by side, inspect an annual crop calendar, review applied agronomic rules, and verify the exact NASA climate indicators backing every recommendation—reducing climate risk while promoting sustainable soil and water management
details:
AgroNASA — Project Documentation

What exactly does it do?

AgroNASA is a web-based agricultural decision-support application designed to help farmers, agronomists, and rural advisors in the province of San Luis, Argentina, design, evaluate, and compare resilient crop rotation strategies adapted to local agroclimatic variability.

Using 26 years of historical satellite and meteorological records from NASA POWER (2000–2025)—cross-referenced with SRTM 30m topography, FAO GAEZ v4 agro-climatic suitability, and FAO-56 / INTA crop parameters—the platform diagnoses the environmental risks of three distinct agroecological zones in San Luis:

North Zone (Valle del Conlara / Sierras): 800–1,200 m.a.s.l., higher root-zone soil moisture (0.597), low summer water stress, but high late-spring frost risk (34.7 frost days/year) and water erosion on slopes.

Central Zone (San Luis Capital / Villa Mercedes): 500–750 m.a.s.l., transitional undulating plains with moderate soil moisture (0.413), summer heatwaves (26.3 days/year ≥35 °C during flowering), and rainfall variability (771 mm/year).

South Zone (Buena Esperanza / Dupuy Dept.): 350–500 m.a.s.l., sandy dune plains with low water retention (0.326), severe summer heat stress (34.0 days/year ≥35 °C), and high susceptibility to wind erosion on bare soils.

Based on the user's geographic zone, soil condition, priority objective, and multi-campaign crop history, AgroNASA generates and ranks tailored crop rotation strategies—complete with qualitative and quantitative resilience indicators, an interactive 12-month planting/harvest timeline, rule-by-rule explanations, and direct NASA satellite evidence.

How does it work?

The platform operates through three tightly integrated layers:

1. Satellite & Climate Data Pipeline (pipeline/ & data/)

Automated Python scripts query the NASA POWER Agroclimatology API across 9,497 daily records (2000–2025) for San Luis reference coordinates.

The pipeline filters missing values (-999), aggregates daily series into 312 monthly records (power_daily.csv and power_monthly.csv), and extracts multi-decadal seasonal indicators (indicadores_estacionales.py): annual and seasonal precipitation, root-zone soil moisture, extreme heat days (≥35 °C), frost frequency, and evapotranspiration stress.

Regional profiles (data/zonas.yaml) and zone-adapted crop catalogs (data/crops.yaml) model each crop's phenological traits: water consumption (mm/cycle), drought tolerance (0–1), atmospheric nitrogen fixation (boolean), root depth (cm), peak soil coverage (0–1), organic matter contribution (%), sowing season (summer, winter, cover), and cycle length (months).

2. Agronomic Simulation & Scoring Engine (Back/app/)

Built on FastAPI and Pydantic, the backend exposes REST endpoints for regions, crops, rotations, and custom simulations.

When a farmer submits their parcel configuration and previous campaign history, ScoringEngine (Back/app/scoring/engine.py) evaluates candidate crop sequences against both the zone's NASA climate profile and agronomic rotation principles:

Monoculture & Soil Depletion Penalties: Detects consecutive campaigns of the same crop family or nutrient-exhausting sequences, triggering alerts for pest pressure, nitrogen depletion, or structural loss.

Legume & Cover Crop Synergies: Rewards sequences that alternate high-carbon grasses (e.g., corn, sorghum, wheat, rye) with nitrogen-fixing legumes (e.g., soybean, vetch) and winter cover crops to protect sandy or sloped soils from wind/water erosion.

Climatic Window Alignment: Matches crop drought tolerance and cycle length against seasonal water deficits, heatwave frequency during flowering, and frost-free windows.

Returns structured strategy options (such as High Productivity, Balanced / Risk Diversification, and Soil Conservation & Recovery) along with qualitative metrics, pros/cons, and explicit calculation rules.

3. Interactive Agronomic Decision Board (Front/src/)

Interactive GIS Map & Parcel Setup (MapSelector.jsx, ConfigForm.jsx): Uses Leaflet to let users click directly on San Luis zones or coordinates, define field parameters, load or save farm profiles (ProfileHistoryModal.jsx), and input multi-year campaign history.

Campaign History Diagnosis (PanelHistorialDecision): A collapsible diagnostic panel that analyzes the farmer's past rotations, highlights cumulative soil/climate impacts, and allows saving the newly chosen strategy into the farm's history.

Strategy Comparison Cards (DecisionBoard.jsx): Displays recommended strategies in either a side-by-side grid or tab selector view, complete with visual performance meters, pros/cons lists, and an interactive Calculation Rules Modal explaining every bonus and penalty applied by the engine.

Annual Crop Calendar (Timeline) & NASA Evidence (EvidenciaNasa): Visualizes month-by-month sowing, growth, and harvest windows for the selected strategy alongside the exact NASA POWER indicators justifying the recommendation.

What benefits does it have?

Scientifically Grounded & Locally Calibrated: Replaces generic national averages and intuition with 26 years of location-specific NASA satellite agroclimatology tailored to San Luis's contrasting North, Central, and South ecosystems.

Proactive Climate Risk Mitigation: Identifies vulnerability to summer heatwaves (≥35 °C), late frosts, and root-zone water deficits before seeds are purchased or planted.

100% Explainable ("No Black Box"): Every strategy card includes an open rules breakdown and NASA evidence metrics so farmers and advisors understand why a rotation is recommended.

Soil Regeneration & Erosion Control: Actively prevents winter bare-soil wind erosion in southern sandy plains and water runoff in northern valleys by integrating winter cover crops and nitrogen-fixing legumes.

Iterative Farm Memory: Allows users to store parcel profiles and campaign histories, turning single-season advice into a multi-year management tool.

What do you hope to achieve?

Short Term: Validate and refine the agronomic ruleset with local producers, INTA extension specialists, and agricultural cooperatives in San Luis to reduce crop losses caused by erratic rainfall and extreme temperatures.

Medium Term: Integrate real-time seasonal climate forecasts (ENSO phases: El Niño / La Niña) and high-resolution satellite soil moisture products (such as NASA SMAP and MODIS NDVI) for dynamic in-season adjustments.

Long Term: Scale the platform across the Argentine Pampas, Gran Chaco, and other semi-arid farming regions in Latin America, adding downloadable PDF technical certificates to support sustainable agricultural credit and climate-risk insurance.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Programming Languages

Python 3.12 (NASA data ingestion pipeline, seasonal statistical analysis, and FastAPI backend engine)

JavaScript (ES6+ / ES Modules), JSX, HTML5, and CSS3 (interactive web client, custom animations, and responsive grid layout)

YAML & JSON (structured agroecological zone profiles, crop trait catalogs, and pre-computed climate indicators)

Frameworks, Libraries & APIs

Frontend:

React 19 (react, react-dom) — Component-based UI and reactive state management

Vite 8 (@vitejs/plugin-react) — High-speed frontend tooling and production bundler

Leaflet 1.9.4 — Interactive geospatial map for agroecological zone selection in San Luis

Oxlint 1.90 — Fast JavaScript/React linter for code quality

Backend:

FastAPI (≥0.110) — High-performance asynchronous REST API

Uvicorn (≥0.29) — ASGI web server

Pydantic (≥2.6) — Strict data validation, serialization, and API contract schemas

PyYAML (≥6.0.1) & python-dotenv (≥1.0.1) — Configuration and catalog parsing

Data Science & Earth Observation Sources:

NASA POWER API (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources) — 26-year daily and monthly agroclimatic time series (2000–2025)

SRTM 30m (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) — Elevation, slope, and erosion risk characterization

FAO GAEZ v4 & FAO-56 / INTA Reference Data — Agro-climatic suitability and crop water/phenology parameters

Pandas (≥2.2) & Requests (≥2.31) — Time-series cleaning, aggregation, and seasonal feature engineering

Software, Hardware & Development Environment

OS & Runtime: Linux development environment, Node.js, npm, and Python venv

Version Control: Git & GitHub for collaborative branching and integration

Browser & Testing: Chrome / Firefox DevTools and FastAPI interactive Swagger UI (/docs) on standard laptop/desktop workstations
